title: Require documented labour and psychological-safety standards for any data-labelling workforce
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on the TIME investigation into OpenAI's use of Kenyan data labellers. Not a documented decision of any specific organisation. Confidence rationale: 'Community' — this concept has no dedicated AI-specific labour framework to anchor to yet (see CTR-020), which is itself an honest governance gap this dataset records rather than papering over.

history.note: Initial Edition 1.1 content, part of the Phase 3 canonical expansion.

decision_statement: Before contracting a third-party workforce (directly or via an outsourcing vendor) to label training or safety-classifier data containing graphic, traumatic, or otherwise psychologically harmful content, the organisation must require documented wage floors, exposure limits, and access to psychological support for that workforce, and must audit the vendor's actual practice, not only its contractual commitments.
decision_context: Motivated by reporting that Kenyan data labellers were paid under $2/hour to review extremely graphic content in order to build OpenAI's content-safety classifier, with workers reporting lasting psychological trauma.
governing_body: Illustrative example — AI Supply Chain Labor Standards Board
frameworks_referenced: ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work
alternatives_considered: Rely on a vendor's own contractual labour commitments without independent audit.
Treat data-labelling labour conditions as entirely the outsourcing vendor's responsibility, outside the client's governance scope.

citations.title: OpenAI Used Kenyan Workers on Less Than $2 Per Hour: Exclusive

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled as a direct governance response to this investigation.
The decision is put into practice via this single, primary design pattern.
Documented wage and psychological-safety standards are a direct application of general ILO labour principles to this specific AI supply-chain context.
Compliance must be demonstrated by an observable vendor welfare audit.
Boards adopting this decision should be asking whether they actually know their data-labelling workforce's conditions.
